etymology: Of uncertain origin, first found in English in the sixteenth century, perhaps imitative. In Nahum 3:2 the participle jumping renders the Hebrew raqad, to skip, leap, dance.
biblical_def: Nahum describes the fall of Nineveh as if the reader stood in its streets. “The noise of a whip, and the noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the pransing horses, and of the jumping chariots” (Nahum 3:2). The chariots bounce and leap over the paving as they charge; Webster cites this very verse under jump, to jolt. The next verse shows where the charge ends: “The horseman lifteth up both the bright sword and the glittering spear: and there is a multitude of slain, and a great number of carcases” (Nahum 3:3). Nahum had already seen it from a distance: “The chariots shall rage in the streets, they shall justle one against another in the broad ways” (Nahum 2:4). Nineveh had sent its chariots jumping through other nations' streets for two centuries. Now the jumping chariots were in her own, and the God of Israel had sent them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): JUMP, verb intransitive 1. To leap; to skip; to spring. Applied to men, it signifies to spring upwards or forwards with both feet, in distinction from hop, which signifies to spring with one foot. A man jumps over a ditch; a beast jumps over a fence.
webster_full: JUMP, verb intransitive 1. To leap; to skip; to spring. Applied to men, it signifies to spring upwards or forwards with both feet, in distinction from hop, which signifies to spring with one foot. A man jumps over a ditch; a beast jumps over a fence. A man jumps upon a horse; a goat jumps from rock to rock.
2. To spring over any thing; to pass to at a leap. Here, upon this bank and shelve of time, We'd jump the life to come. We see a little, presume a great deal, and so jump to the conclusion.
3. To bound; to pass from object to object; to jolt. The noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the prancing horses, and of the jumping chariots. Nahum 3.
4. To agree; to tally; to coincide. In some sort it jumps with my humor. [This use of the word is now vulgar, and in America, I think, is confined to the single phrase, to jump in judgment.
JUMP, verb transitive To pass by a leap; to pass over eagerly or hastily; as, to jump a stream. [But over is understood.]

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God repays the violent in kind. The empire that lived by the chariot fell by the chariot, exactly as the prophet foretold.

pos: v.i. (to make a quick, sharp, repeated noise)
etymology: Middle English ratelen, imitative of the sound, related to Dutch ratelen. In Job 39:23 it renders the Hebrew ranah, to rattle, to ring; in Nahum 3:2 rattling renders ra'ash, quaking, shaking.
biblical_def: God's questions to Job include a portrait of the war-horse, and the sound is part of the picture. “Hast thou given the horse strength? hast thou clothed his neck with thunder?” (Job 39:19). The horse charges toward the weapons, not away from them: “The quiver rattleth against him, the glittering spear and the shield” (Job 39:23). Arrows rattle in the rider's quiver at every stride, and the animal only grows bolder: “He saith among the trumpets, Ha, ha; and he smelleth the battle afar off, the thunder of the captains, and the shouting” (Job 39:25). The point of the portrait is not the horse but its Maker. Job cannot give the horse its courage, and he cannot answer God. Nahum hears the other side of the noise in the street of a falling city, “the noise of the rattling of the wheels” (Nahum 3:2). The rattle of war is under God's hand in both places.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): RAT'TLE, verb intransitive 1. To make a quick sharp noise rapidly repeated, by the collision of bodies not very sonorous. When bodies are sonorous, it is called jingling. We say, the wheels rattle over the pavement. And the rude hail in rattling tempest forms.
webster_full: RAT'TLE, verb intransitive 1. To make a quick sharp noise rapidly repeated, by the collision of bodies not very sonorous. When bodies are sonorous, it is called jingling. We say, the wheels rattle over the pavement. And the rude hail in rattling tempest forms.
2. To speak eagerly and noisily; to utter words in a clattering manner. Thus turbulent in rattling tone she spoke. He rattles it out against popery.
RAT'TLE, verb transitive 1. To cause to make a rattling sound or a rapid succession of sharp sounds; as, to rattle a chain.
2. To stun with noise; to drive with sharp sounds rapidly repeated. Sound but another, and another shall, as loud as thine, rattle the welkin's ear.
3. To scold; to rail at clamorously; as, to rattle off servants sharply.
scriptures: The quiver rattleth against him, the glittering spear and the shield.

Nah 3:2
The noise of a whip, and the noise of the rattling of the wheels, and of the pransing horses, and of the jumping chariots.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain and imitative. The war-horse passage is sometimes read as nature poetry for its own sake, but in context it is part of God's answer to Job, showing that the creature's strength and courage are the Creator's gift.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the humbling of man before the works of God. Job could not clothe a horse's neck with thunder, and he laid his hand upon his mouth.

pos: v.i. (to make a low, heavy, continued sound)
etymology: Middle English romblen, imitative, related to Dutch rommelen. In Jeremiah 47:3 the noun rumbling renders the Hebrew hamon, a noise, tumult, roar.
biblical_def: Jeremiah's oracle against the Philistines begins with a flood from the north: “Behold, waters rise up out of the north, and shall be an overflowing flood, and shall overflow the land” (Jeremiah 47:2). The flood is an army, and the prophet makes the reader hear it coming: “At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his strong horses, at the rushing of his chariots, and at the rumbling of his wheels, the fathers shall not look back to their children for feebleness of hands” (Jeremiah 47:3). Terror is so complete that fathers abandon their children. The reason is given plainly: “for the LORD will spoil the Philistines, the remnant of the country of Caphtor” (Jeremiah 47:4). The rumbling of Babylon's wheels was the sound of God's judgment approaching Gaza and Ashkelon, and no wall could keep it out.

corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. The oracles against the nations are often skipped as obscure, but they teach that the God of Israel is the judge of all the earth, and that every nation answers to Him.

pos: v.t. (to outrun; to overflow, run over)
etymology: From over and run, Old English ofer-irnan. In 2 Samuel 18:23 it renders the Hebrew 'abar, to pass by, pass beyond; in Nahum 1:8 overrunning renders the same verb, of a flood passing over.
biblical_def: The word appears in two very different scenes. After Absalom's death, Ahimaaz begged to carry the news to David though Joab had already sent the Cushite. “But howsoever, said he, let me run. And he said unto him, Run. Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and overran Cushi” (2 Samuel 18:23). He outran the official messenger by taking the longer but easier road, and arrived first with nothing to say about the king's son. In Nahum the word describes judgment: “But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof, and darkness shall pursue his enemies” (Nahum 1:8). Nineveh was in fact taken when the rivers rose and breached its walls. Yet the verse before is the comfort of the faithful: “The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him” (Nahum 1:7). The same God who sends the overrunning flood is the refuge of those who trust Him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): OVERRUN ', verb transitive 1. To run or spread over; to grow over; to cover all over. The sluggard's farm is overrun with weeds. Some plants unchecked will soon overrun a field.
webster_full: OVERRUN ', verb transitive 1. To run or spread over; to grow over; to cover all over. The sluggard's farm is overrun with weeds. Some plants unchecked will soon overrun a field. The Canada thistle is overrunning the northern parts of New England, as it has overrun Normandy.
2. To march or rove over; to harass by hostile incursions; to ravage. The south of Europe was formerly overrun by the Goths, Vandals and other barbarians.
3. To outrun; to run faster than another and leave him behind. Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and overran Cushi. 2 Samuel 18:1.
4. To overspread with numbers. Were it not for the ibis, it has been supposed Egypt would be overrun with crocodiles.
5. To injure by treading down.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. Ahimaaz is sometimes held up as a model of zeal; the narrative presents him rather as a man eager to run with no message to bring, a warning to every messenger who outruns his commission.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold: a messenger must carry the word he is given, and the LORD who overruns His enemies like a flood is a strong hold to those who trust Him.

pos: v.t. (to cross back and forth; to wander across)
etymology: Old French traverser, from Latin transversare, to cross, from trans and vertere, to turn. In Jeremiah 2:23 traversing renders the Hebrew sarak, to entangle, to run hither and thither.
biblical_def: Jeremiah answers Judah's denial of idolatry with an image from the desert. “How canst thou say, I am not polluted, I have not gone after Baalim? see thy way in the valley, know what thou hast done: thou art a swift dromedary traversing her ways” (Jeremiah 2:23). A young she-camel in season runs back and forth, crossing and recrossing her own tracks, restless and driven. The next image is coarser still: “A wild ass used to the wilderness, that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure; in her occasion who can turn her away?” (Jeremiah 2:24). Judah ran after the gods of the nations with the same appetite. The LORD had stated the charge at the start: “For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13). Traversing is the motion of a heart that has left the fountain and cannot rest anywhere else.

1. Something that thwarts, crosses or obstructs; a cross accident. He is satisfied he should have succeeded, had it not been for unlucky traverses not in his power.
2. In fortification, a trench with a little parapet for protecting men on the flank; also, a wall raised across a work.

corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. Jeremiah's animal imagery is blunt by design, and modern readers who find it offensive have missed that idolatry is spiritual adultery and that God speaks of it in the language it deserves.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the restlessness of the idolatrous heart. Augustine's confession that our heart is restless till it rests in God is Jeremiah's point turned into prayer.

pos: v.i. (to glitter, to flash with points of light)
etymology: From spark, Old English spearca, with the frequentative -le. In Ezekiel 1:7 it renders the Hebrew natsats, to gleam, glitter.
biblical_def: Ezekiel's first vision opens by the river Chebar with a storm of fire. “And I looked, and, behold, a whirlwind came out of the north, a great cloud, and a fire infolding itself, and a brightness was about it, and out of the midst thereof as the colour of amber, out of the midst of the fire” (Ezekiel 1:4). Out of it came four living creatures, and the prophet records even their feet: “And their feet were straight feet; and the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf's foot: and they sparkled like the colour of burnished brass” (Ezekiel 1:7). The cherubim flash with the reflected glory of the One enthroned above them. John saw the same burnished brightness in the risen Christ: “And his feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace; and his voice as the sound of many waters” (Revelation 1:15). The sparkle of the creatures is borrowed light; the brightness of the Son is His own.
webster_full: SP'ARKLE, noun 1. A spark.
2. A luminous particle.
SP'ARKLE, verb intransitive 1. To emit sparks; to send off small ignited particles; as burning fuel, etc.
2. To glitter; to glisten; as, a brilliant sparkles; sparkling colors.
3. To twinkle; to glitter; as sparkling stars.

corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. Ezekiel's vision has been made the basis of fanciful speculation, including modern claims that it describes a spacecraft. Scripture calls it the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD (Ezekiel 1:28), and it is to be received as revelation, not decoded as technology.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is reverence before the glory of God. Ezekiel fell upon his face; the sparkling creatures were the servants of a throne.

pos: n. (a layer, a fold of flesh)
etymology: Middle English flake, of Scandinavian origin, related to Norwegian flak, a flat piece. In Job 41:23 it renders the Hebrew mappal, a fold, a falling part, the dewlap.
biblical_def: God's description of leviathan includes its armour of flesh as well as of scales. “His scales are his pride, shut up together as with a close seal” (Job 41:15). Beneath the scales the folds of the body are equally hard: “The flakes of his flesh are joined together: they are firm in themselves; they cannot be moved” (Job 41:23). Webster cites this verse for flake as a layer or stratum of flesh. The creature is invulnerable to man's weapons, and that is the lesson. If no man dare stir up leviathan, who can stand before the One who made him? God asks it directly: “Who hath prevented me, that I should repay him? whatsoever is under the whole heaven is mine” (Job 41:11). The flakes of leviathan's flesh, joined and immovable, are a sermon on the strength of the Creator and the folly of contending with Him.

2. A platform of hurdles, or small sticks made fast or interwoven, supported by stanchions, on which cod-fish is dried.
3. A layer or stratum; as a flake of flesh or tallow. Job 41:23.
4. A collection or little particle of fire, or of combustible matter on fire, separated and flying off.
5. Any scaly matter in layers; any mass cleaving off in scales. Little flakes of scurf.

pos: n. (a step; the length of a stride)
etymology: Old French pas, from Latin passus, a step, stride, from pandere, to stretch. In 2 Samuel 6:13 it renders the Hebrew tsa'ad, a step.
biblical_def: The second attempt to bring the ark to Jerusalem began with six steps. The first attempt had ended in death: the ark was carried on a cart, Uzzah put out his hand to steady it, “and God smote him there for his error; and there he died by the ark of God” (2 Samuel 6:7). David learned that the ark must be carried as God commanded, on the shoulders of the Levites. So the second time: “And it was so, that when they that bare the ark of the LORD had gone six paces, he sacrificed oxen and fatlings” (2 Samuel 6:13). Six paces, and God had not struck; the king stopped and worshipped. Then came the joy: “And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod” (2 Samuel 6:14). Six paces taken God's way were worth more than a whole procession taken man's way.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PACE, noun [Latin, to open, Gr., to tread. See Pass.] 1. A step.
webster_full: PACE, noun [Latin, to open, Gr., to tread. See Pass.] 1. A step.

2. The space between the two feet in walking, estimated at two feet and a half. But the geometrical pace is five feet, or the whole space passed over by the same foot from one step to another. Sixty thousand such paces make one degree on the equator.
3. Manner of walking; a gait; as a languishing pace; a heavy pace; a quick or slow pace
4. Step; gradation in business. [Little Used.]
5. A mode of stepping among horses, in which the legs on the same side are lifted together. In a general sense, the word may be applied to any other mode of stepping.
scriptures: And it was so, that when they that bare the ark of the LORD had gone six paces, he sacrificed oxen and fatlings.
And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah; and God smote him there for his error; and there he died by the ark of God.
And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod.
corruption_summary: David's dancing before the ark is used to license innovation in worship, when the chapter's lesson is that God must be approached in the way He commands.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary worship movements cite David dancing with all his might as warrant for liturgical dance and every innovation of enthusiasm. They pass over the first half of the chapter, where Uzzah died because the ark was moved on a new cart instead of by the Levites, as the law required (Numbers 4:15; 1 Chronicles 15:13).

The principle to recover is the regulative principle. Joy before God is commanded, but the manner of approach is His to appoint, and the six paces were taken by Levites carrying the ark as God had said.

etymology: From on and -ward, Old English -weard, toward. In Exodus 40:36 it renders the Hebrew nasa', to pull up stakes, set out, journey.
biblical_def: Exodus ends with the tabernacle raised and filled with the glory of the LORD, and with a rule for the whole journey. “And when the cloud was taken up from over the tabernacle, the children of Israel went onward in all their journeys” (Exodus 40:36). The cloud moved; Israel moved. “But if the cloud were not taken up, then they journeyed not till the day that it was taken up” (Exodus 40:37). They did not set the pace or choose the road. “For the cloud of the LORD was upon the tabernacle by day, and fire was on it by night, in the sight of all the house of Israel, throughout all their journeys” (Exodus 40:38). Onward, for Israel, meant forward under God's visible guidance and never ahead of it. The church now has no pillar of cloud, but it has the word that is a lamp to the feet, and it goes onward only as far and as fast as that word leads.

2. In a state of advanced progression.

2. Increased; improved.

corruption_summary: Onward is the cry of activism and progress, when Israel went onward only when the cloud was taken up.
corruption_paragraphs: The word is the anthem of every movement that equates motion with faithfulness, from the hymn Onward, Christian Soldiers to every vision-casting program that urges the church forward without asking where God has told it to go.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is guidance by God's word. Israel's onward march was strictly governed: they journeyed when the cloud moved and rested when it rested.
roots_summary: On plus -ward, toward; rendering Hebrew nasa', to set out, at Exodus 40:36.
roots_lines: Old English on, on, and -weard, toward.
Hebrew nasa', to pull up tent-pegs, to journey.
Exodus 40:36 says Israel went onward when the cloud was taken up.
Exodus 40:37 says they journeyed not until it was taken up.
Exodus 40:38 places the cloud and fire over the tabernacle throughout their journeys.
usage: the children of Israel went onward in all their journeys
forward under the cloud
never ahead of God's guidance

etymology: From there and into, Old English thaer and in to. In Luke 21:21 it renders the Greek eis auten, into it.
biblical_def: In the Olivet discourse the Lord gave His disciples a sign and a command concerning Jerusalem. “And when ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies, then know that the desolation thereof is nigh” (Luke 21:20). The command was to flee, and not to go back: “Then let them which are in Judaea flee to the mountains; and let them which are in the midst of it depart out; and let not them that are in the countries enter thereinto” (Luke 21:21). The city that killed the prophets was under sentence: “For these be the days of vengeance, that all things which are written may be fulfilled” (Luke 21:22). Eusebius records that the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by revelation, left the city for Pella before the Roman siege of AD 70. They did not enter thereinto, and they were spared. Obedience to Christ's plain word was their deliverance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): THEREINTO ', adverb [there and into.] Into that.
webster_full: THEREINTO ', adverb [there and into.] Into that.
The word occurs once in the Authorized Version, at Luke 21:21.
It renders the Greek eis auten, into it.
Christ forbade those in the countries to enter Jerusalem when it was compassed with armies.
It is formed like thereof, therein and thereto.

corruption_summary: Luke 21:20-24 is pushed wholly into a future tribulation, when Christ's warning was fulfilled in the Roman siege of Jerusalem in AD 70.
corruption_paragraphs: Dispensational teaching assigns the Olivet discourse almost entirely to a seven-year tribulation still to come. Luke's account is plain that the compassing armies and the desolation concern the destruction of Jerusalem in that generation, which came in AD 70. The dictionary holds partial preterism within orthodoxy on this passage and rejects dispensational premillennialism.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reliability of Christ's prophecy and the safety of obeying it. Those who did not enter thereinto lived.
roots_summary: There plus into; rendering Greek eis auten, into it, at Luke 21:21.
